title: Simulated Annealing (Bertsimas, Tsitsiklis), chapter 2 of Probability and Algorithms (National Research Council 1992), National Academies Press read-online text
contribution: The 1992 printing of the simulated-annealing review that Statistical Science printed in 1993 (S005), as chapter 2 of the National Research Council report Probability and Algorithms: the same text and verdicts word for word apart from copy-editing, so the review's verdicts date from 1992.
problem_entry: HS+SD, as S005 (card c01, not re-carded): 'Our goal in this review is to describe the method, its convergence, and its behavior in applications' (p. 1). Venue: a chapter of a National Research Council panel survey of probability and algorithms (S438, card a3-01; Bertsimas sat on the panel per that card), not a statistics journal. First-page check: title, both authors, MIT (p. 1).
key_idea: Not re-carded (S005, card c01). Card's comparison: a word-level sequence comparison (difflib) of the text before the references matches 3,369 of 3,514 B020 tokens with S005 (ratio 0.93; the item note reports 3,298 of 3,411, ratio 0.94, with another tokenization); unmatched tokens are mostly formula fragments. Differences 1992 -> 1993: S005 adds journal header, key words and an author note (Associate Professors, Sloan and EECS); 'Kirkpatrick et al. (1983)' expanded; 'it happens at a minimum energy configuration' becomes 'this happens'; citations alphabetized and et al. expanded; sections 2.1-2.3 and Theorem 2.1 renumbered 1-3 and Theorem 1; nine occurrences of 'simulated annealing' (pp. 2, 6, 7, 8) abbreviated to SA; the relaxation-time expression '|log(1 -λ2)|' (p. 5) absent from S005's extracted text (page image not checked); small copy-edits (i.e./that is, namely, van Laarhoven, gridpoint) (pp. 1, 5, 7-10).
assumptions: Same as S005: finite set, symmetric neighbourhoods, nonincreasing cooling schedule, irreducible aperiodic chains (pp. 1-3); the formulas are images missing from this text (pp. 2, 4-6).
proof_devices: Not re-carded: the surveyed devices are S005's (card c01), word for word here: Hajek's convergence theorem, the relaxation-time reading, singular perturbation with large-deviation bounds, the random-walk and exhaustive-search checks, Sasaki-Hajek and Hajek's separable example (pp. 3-8).
experiments: Not re-carded: S005's report of Johnson et al. (graph partitioning at equal computation time, colouring, TSP; cooling schedules) is word for word here (pp. 8-10); no experiments of their own.
positioning: Same credits as S005; the reference lists hold the same 36 works (card's count); two are Tsitsiklis's own (1988, 1989), none is Bertsimas's (p. 13). Johnson et al. Part III is 'in preparation' in 1992 (p. 12), an 'Unpublished manuscript' in 1993 (S005 p. 5); Laud et al. 1989 cited with 'Revised version to appear in J. Stoch. Opt. (1992)' (p. 12).
writing: In 1992 the method is named in full in nine places where the 1993 text abbreviates (pp. 2, 6-8); the 1993 edits look like journal house style (alphabetical citations, full author lists, key words, author note) [inferred from the pattern of edits].
limits_future: Same as S005: finite sets only; calls for complexity results, rapid mixing at low temperature, a theory of cooling schedules and more experiments (pp. 6-10). Dating: the text and both verdicts were in print in 1992 (year from the report's record, S438 and works.json; NAP doi 10.17226/2026), a year before Statistical Science 8(1); the references fit (latest items 1992, in preparation or to appear, p. 12).

method_links.note: Dating only; version pair of S005, do not count twice: the review judges SA by guarantees and reports the comparison by Johnson et al. at equal computation time, so the stated yardstick that C8 dates to 1993 [S005 pp. 3-4] is in print in 1992; still a yardstick applied to experiments by others, not his practice (C8 unchanged).

Dating only (also the Domain Map HS row and C15): the 1993 verdict (theory lacking, practice mixed, generally applicable and easy to implement) is already in the 1992 NRC printing; read 1993 as 1992 (NRC report), reprinted 1993 (Stat. Sci.). Content unchanged.

transferable: None new: S005's (card c01) hold for the 1992 text: test a stochastic search's guarantee against exhaustive search and a fixed-temperature random walk (p. 6); judge it by hitting time as a function of instance size (p. 6); compare it with the best specialized heuristic at equal computation time (p. 9).

quotes.text: As far as theory is concerned, there is at present a definite lack of rigorous results justifying the use of simulated annealing.

Overall, SA is a generally applicable and easy-to-implement probabilistic approximation algorithm that is able to produce good solutions for an optimization problem, even if we do not understand the structure of the problem well.

title: Introduction to Linear Optimization (Bertsimas, Tsitsiklis; Athena Scientific 1997): Preface, as served on the publisher's web page
contribution: The joint preface of Introduction to Linear Optimization (1997), read in full in its web form: insight first through the interplay of geometry and algebra, comprehensive but economical, structure kept apart from the simplex method, a closing chapter on the art of linear optimization, and a book grown from a first-year graduate course at MIT.
problem_entry: LO+IO (with finance, stochastic programming, HS and AP case studies as topics): 'a unified, insightful, and modern treatment of linear optimization, that is, linear programming, network flow problems, and discrete linear optimization', with 'special attention to theory' plus applications and case studies; main objective 'a sophisticated practitioner of (linear) optimization, or a researcher', through four abilities in order: formulate fairly complex problems, appreciate 'the main classes of problems that are practically solvable', describe the solution methods, understand qualitative properties of solutions (p. 1, purpose paragraph).
key_idea: Stated philosophy: 'insight matters most', which 'necessarily requires a geometric view', while algorithms 'can only be described algebraically'; hence 'the beautiful interplay between algebra and geometry' (p. 1). Also 'comprehensive, but economical'; state of the art (interior point, large scale, case studies 'that stretch the limits of currently available algorithms and computers'); the art chapter 'a critical part of this book'. Three departures: the tableau only 'a useful device for working out numerical examples'; general form instead of standard form; 'we separate the structural understanding of linear programming from the particulars of the simplex method', with duality not relying on simplex. A cross-chapter theme: problems with exponentially many constraints (sections 10.3, 8.5, ch. 6, case study 12.5) (all p. 1).
assumptions: Prerequisite 'a working knowledge of linear algebra', a small subset 'sometimes used in subtle ways'; mathematical maturity helps; audience a first-year graduate course at MIT for engineering and operations research students (p. 1, course paragraph). Scope: linear and discrete linear optimization; no nonlinear or conic topic named (p. 1).
proof_devices: Duality proved twice: 'first obtained as a corollary of the simplex method', then from a separating hyperplane theorem developed from first principles (p. 1, Chapter 4 paragraph)
Dual optimal solutions characterized as subgradients of an optimal cost function (p. 1, Chapter 5 paragraph)
'a proof of the polynomiality of linear programming' via the ellipsoid method; equivalence of separation and optimization; problems with exponentially many constraints (p. 1, Chapter 8 paragraph)
Convergence proofs and complexity analysis of interior point methods (p. 1, Chapter 9 paragraph)
A duality theory for integer programming (p. 1, Chapter 11 paragraph)
Network flows: the major algorithmic ideas 'rather than on the refinements that can lead to better complexity estimates' (p. 1, Chapter 7 paragraph)
experiments: Chapter 12 compares interior point methods with simplex variants 'in a realistic large scale setting' and gives 'some indication of the size of problems that can be currently solved' (p. 1). Exercises are 'intended to deepen the understanding of the subject, or to explore extensions of the theory in the text, as opposed to routine drills'; some numerical; starred ones fairly hard; a solutions manual for qualified instructors (p. 1). No numbers in the preface.
positioning: Departs from 'many other textbooks' (tableau as the central topic; standard form); lists topics 'not commonly covered' (column geometry, duality and the pricing of financial assets, a unified view of delayed column generation and cutting planes, stochastic programming and Benders, the auction algorithm, ellipsoid implications, interior point methods, a chapter on practice) (p. 1). No comprehensive bibliography: historical originals, recent texts and recent journal articles (p. 1). Thanks colleagues Dimitri Bertsekas (the person the skill distinguishes from Bertsimas) and Rob Freund (later S128 coauthor) and 15 named readers, seven of them Bertsimas coauthors in works.json: Chryssikou, Gamarnik, Mourtzinou, Paschalidis, Perakis, Sethuraman, Stock (card's count) (p. 1).
writing: First-person plural objectives in sequence ('Our general philosophy', 'Another of our objectives', 'Our last objective'); one paragraph per departure, each with its reason (the standard form 'can hinder the deeper understanding of the subject'); a chapter-by-chapter description, modularity guidance and four course plans; one hedge, 'It will, we hope, convince the reader' (p. 1).
limits_future: Stated limits: not encyclopedic; no comprehensive bibliography; much of ch. 5-6 rarely used later; ch. 9 not used later except in some ch. 12 applications; starred sections hold material 'not usually covered in an introductory course' (p. 1). Four course designs, two tried at MIT, incl. a half-course on IP (p. 1). Comparison: the Chapter 11 paragraph names no complexity-theory section, though the printed contents has section 11.8 (B004 p. 5). The web text (Last-Modified 1999-11-04) was not checked against the printed preface (book p. xi), which is not open.

method_links.note: Stated jointly, now card-level (was web-sourced, 02 T8, W6): geometry first, then algebra and algorithms; structure kept apart from the simplex method; strong formulations (Chapter 10 paragraph). Joint book material: framing and dating only; do not add to the say-do counts; book material never promotes.

The Voice entry (textbook-era taste) rests on a joint 1997 preface now read in full; geometry before algebra is stated; LP as the engine of relaxations is not stated here (only exercise bounds for IP problems and the unified view of column generation and cutting planes).

Dating: the row's strong formulations, stated 1998 and 2005, have a joint 1997 antecedent: the Chapter 10 intuition for a strong formulation, and section 10.2 Guidelines for strong formulations (B004 p. 4); the 1998 statement is S015 p. 2.
The test is stated jointly in 1997 (Quote 2), without naming Dantzig (cited in DMD and RAO, 02 T5).
Order of this PhD text: theory first, art and case studies in the last chapter; problems and data first is the order of the MBA and analytics books (02 P1 era note).

Framing: the four abilities put formulation first and the practically solvable classes second; LP read structurally (general form, duality without simplex, dual solutions as subgradients, duality and the pricing of financial assets), matching step 4. Joint book material: framing and dating only; do not add to the say-do counts; book material never promotes.

Limitations dating (also C19, Warning sign 2, Taste mark 2): in 1997 the joint text holds both senses of tractable, practically solvable classes, case studies at the limits of current computers and the size of problems currently solvable beside complexity, the ellipsoid method and polynomiality; neither is ranked above the other, so the solve-time sense has a 1997 co-authored antecedent while its statement as the test still dates from 2014 (C19 stands). Joint book material: framing and dating only; do not add to the say-do counts; book material never promotes.

Course to book, stated jointly in 1997: developed while the authors took turns teaching a first-year graduate course at MIT; coauthor a colleague, not a former student; manuscript readers later became his coauthors. Joint book material: framing and dating only; do not add to the say-do counts; book material never promotes.

Audience: the 1997 PhD text is organized by theory and methods (simplex, duality, network algorithms, ellipsoid, interior point, IP methods) with applications gathered in the last chapter; the rejection of methods-first teaching (02 T9) comes from the 2004 and 2016 MBA and analytics books (cf. card S128, a3-02).
Framing (also Domain Map HS): in 1997 simulated annealing is taught as one IP heuristic, beside exact and approximation methods (Chapter 11 paragraph).

Coverage update, not a contradiction of any method: the statements that book prefaces were not read and that the LO voice and the textbooks' philosophy stay web-sourced no longer hold for S002; the preface is read in full in its web form; printed preface and body not read; the Signature Work Anatomy note on unread prefaces is outdated for this book. Field boundary consistent: stochastic programming appears only as a decomposable LP structure with Benders decomposition (Chapter 6 paragraph).
Tsitsiklis as the LO-textbook coauthor; seven of the fifteen thanked readers are later Bertsimas coauthors (works.json).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exponentially many constraints as a recurring object, carried through modeling, complexity, algorithms and a case study
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The preface's cross-chapter theme (modeling 10.3, complexity 8.5, algorithms ch. 6 and 8.5, case study 12.5). Research cards with the same object: lifted formulations replacing exponentially many conservation inequalities [S237 pp. 7-8, 11-12]; LP duality collapsing exponentially many subset constraints [S031 pp. 15-16]. Book material alone never promotes: candidate pool only.

transferable: Name the reader's target role and its abilities in priority order: formulate, know the practically solvable classes, know the methods, read the solutions' properties (p. 1).
Build each idea from a figure or geometric argument, then translate it into an algebraic formula and an algorithm (p. 1).
Define key concepts in the general form of the problem and specialize to a standard form only for algorithms, so readers know which properties hold generally (p. 1).
Derive a structural result (duality) apart from the algorithm that first yields it (p. 1).
Carry one structural theme across chapters, from modeling through complexity and algorithms to a case study, and say where each step sits (p. 1).
Write exercises that deepen or extend the theory rather than drill; star the hard ones and say which sections are skippable (p. 1).

title: Introduction to Linear Optimization: publisher web pages (Athena Scientific book page with review excerpts, Athena contents page, Dynamic Ideas book page)
contribution: Publisher pages of Introduction to Linear Optimization: Athena's description, six special features and praise-only review excerpts (Ramana, Bard), a web contents list that lacks the printed section 11.8 Complexity theory, and the Dynamic Ideas page that calls the book PhD-level and reprints the preface's philosophy.
problem_entry: LO+IO. Athena (p. 1): 'This book provides a unified, insightful, and modern treatment of linear optimization, that is, linear programming, network flow problems, and discrete optimization.', the preface's sentence with 'discrete optimization' for 'discrete linear optimization' (B001 p. 1). Dynamic Ideas (p. 3): 'at the PhD level', 'all the recent developments in the field in the last ten years'; 'It emphasizes the underlying geometry, intuition and applications of large scale systems.' The same paragraph is on his own Published Books page (B008 pp. 1-2, checked by text search).
key_idea: Athena's six special features in order: algorithms and duality 'through a geometric perspective'; interior point geometry, convergence and complexity; network-flow methods; 'a detailed treatment of integer programming formulations and algorithms'; 'the art of formulating and solving large scale problems through practical case studies'; examples and exercises 'developed through extensive classroom use in graduate courses' (p. 1). Dynamic Ideas reprints preface paragraphs 2-4 as 'Educational Philosophy' and 5-8 as 'Distinguishing Characteristics' word for word (only 'sub-modular' for 'submodular'), and replaces the chapter-by-chapter description and the exponential-constraints theme paragraph by one general sentence (Quote 2) (p. 3; card's token comparison with B001 p. 1).
assumptions: None stated beyond 'at the PhD level' (p. 3).
experiments: n/a; publisher: 'developed through extensive classroom use in graduate courses' (p. 1).
positioning: Review excerpts chosen by the publisher (p. 1): three sentences of Ramana's Optima 54 review, all praise (pedagogy; geometric and intuitive explanations; 'an outstanding textbook'), none of his criticisms (B005 pp. 13-14), with his 'quailities' corrected to 'qualities'; Jonathan Bard (Interfaces 30(4), July 2000): 'at the top of the list' of 'at least a half dozen new books on linear optimization', 'a comprehensive treatise' (full review not open, not read). Bibliographic: ISBN-10 1-886529-19-1, ISBN-13 978-1-886529-19-9, 1997, 608 pages, hardcover; errata link 'Errata (last updated 7/5/2021)' (B003, another batch) (p. 1).
writing: Publisher feature lists and a three-sentence description (pp. 1, 3); the authors' words appear only as reused preface text under publisher headings (p. 3). Voices: publishers (descriptions, features, contents), reviewers (excerpts), authors (reused preface); Dynamic Ideas is his own company (01 section 1.9), so the p. 3 description is not an independent voice [inferred].
limits_future: Web contents (p. 2) against printed contents (B004 pp. 2-5), line by line (card's): same 12 chapters and section titles except three lines: 1.8 'History, notes, notes and sources' (web) vs 'History, notes, and sources'; no 'Complexity theory' section in the web ch. 11 (print 11.8, book p. 514); 12.2 'Optimization libraries and general observations' vs 'Linear optimization libraries and general observations'. No page numbers or stars on the web. The missing section is the one Ramana calls 'out of the blue' (B005 p. 14); the web preface does not name it either (B001 p. 1); why is not known.

method_links.note: Publisher framing, not independent of B001: the first special feature is a geometric perspective for algorithms and duality; his own press prints the 'insight matters most' paragraph as the book's Educational Philosophy.

Anchor data (ISBN, 1997, 608 pages) and the PhD-level description, also on his own books page (B008); the publisher quotes only praise, the criticisms are on card B005 (Cautions; 05 section 6); Bard's 2000 review known by excerpt only.

Weak, publisher's voice: developed through classroom use in graduate courses and now published by his own press (steps 4-5). Joint book material: framing and dating only; do not add to the say-do counts; book material never promotes.

title: Introduction to Linear Optimization: title page and table of contents (library scan, TU Ilmenau via GBV)
contribution: The printed table of contents of Introduction to Linear Optimization (1997), titles only: 12 chapters and 112 sections, geometry before the simplex method, the simplex-free duality starred, network flows the longest chapter, IP formulations with a strong-formulation section before the IP methods, and three case studies in the closing art chapter.
problem_entry: LO+IO (HS and AP sections): nine LO chapters, two IO chapters (10 formulations, 11 methods), one practice chapter (12) (pp. 2-5). First-page check: title, both authors, MIT, Athena Scientific, Belmont, Massachusetts (p. 1). Preface book p. xi, References book p. 569, Index book p. 579 (pp. 2, 5).
key_idea: Title-level architecture (card's counts from book pages): ch. 2 geometry before ch. 3 simplex, which opens with optimality conditions (pp. 2-3); duality after simplex, with the separating-hyperplane route (4.7) and general LP duality (4.10) starred (p. 3); shares of 568 chapter pages: LP core ch. 1-5 230 pp. (40%), network flows 94 pp. (17%, longest), ch. 8-9 92 pp. (16%), IP 82 pp. (14%), the art 36 pp. (6%); complexity threaded from 1.6 operation counts through 3.7 and ch. 8 to 11.8 complexity theory (pp. 2-5); 10.2 Guidelines for strong formulations before the IP methods; IP duality the longest section of ch. 11 (13 pp.); local search 1 p. and simulated annealing 2 pp. (pp. 4-5).
assumptions: Title-level: linear algebra background as section 1.5 (p. 2); uncertainty only as 6.5 stochastic programming and Benders decomposition, 6 pp. (p. 3); no section title names nonlinear or semidefinite optimization, queueing or stochastic processes (pp. 2-5).
proof_devices: Title-level only: two routes to LP duality, the duality theorem (4.3) and from separating hyperplanes (4.7, starred) (p. 3)
Farkas' lemma (4.6) and representation of polyhedra (2.7 starred, 4.9) (pp. 2-3)
Ellipsoid method for feasibility and optimization (8.3-8.4); problems with exponentially many constraints (8.5, starred, 7 pp.) (p. 4)
IP duality (11.4, 13 pp.), approximation algorithms (11.5) and complexity theory (11.8, 8 pp.) (p. 5)
experiments: Title-level: computational efficiency of the simplex method (3.7), linear optimization libraries and general observations (12.2), three case studies: fleet assignment, air traffic flow management, job shop scheduling (12.3-12.5; the last, 11 pp., is the case study of the exponential-constraints theme) (pp. 3, 5). Two of the three are problems he published on: air traffic flow management (S015, 1998) and job shop scheduling (S130, 1999; S205, 2002) [inferred from titles]. No benchmark visible from titles.
positioning: Every chapter ends with exercises and a notes-and-sources section (ch. 1 'History, notes, and sources'); all but ch. 1 and ch. 9 have a Summary (ch. 9 'An overview'); References book pp. 569-578 (pp. 2-5). Comparison: the Athena web contents differ in three lines (card B002). Metadata note [inferred]: works.json's S002 venue string from Google Scholar carries the page range 479-530, which matches ch. 11 (book pp. 479-532, p. 5): probably a Scholar artifact.
writing: Uniform apparatus: summary, exercises, notes and sources per chapter; eight starred sections (2.7, 2.8, 4.7, 4.10, 5.3, 7.7, 8.5, 9.2) mark advanced material (pp. 2-5; B001 p. 1).
limits_future: Titles only; no chapter content is claimed. The simplex-free duality the preface stresses is a starred, advanced section, and the preface's overview course takes only 4.1-4.3 (p. 3; B001 p. 1) [title-level + preface].

Its 02 W6 part (structure apart from simplex): the simplex-free duality (4.7) and general LP duality (4.10) are starred, advanced sections; the main path derives duality after the simplex method (title-level + B001).

Joint book material: framing and dating only; do not add to the say-do counts; book material never promotes.

title: Review of Introduction to Linear Optimization by Motakuri V. Ramana, Optima 54 (June 1997), pp. 13-14
contribution: Motakuri V. Ramana's signed review in Optima 54 (June 1997), the reviewer's voice for peer critique: praise for the pedagogy, the geometric and intuitive explanations and chapters 8, 9 and 12, with six criticisms (no upper-bounded simplex, uncapacitated network simplex first, an overloaded chapter 7, a brisk chapter 6, the Gomory proof omitted, a complexity section 'out of the blue').
problem_entry: Reviewer's framing, LO+IO: Athena Scientific specializes in books by MIT faculty based on courses taught there; LP treated 'both extensively and thoroughly', network, large-scale and integer optimization 'receive concise treatments'; suitable for a first-year graduate course for doctoral and mathematically inclined master's students in OR, CS, applied mathematics and management science (p. 13). First-page check: running head, title, 'D. Bertsimas and J.N. Tsitsiklis', ISBN (p. 13); signed '-MOTAKURI V. RAMANA' (p. 14).
key_idea: The reviewer: 'The true merit of this book' is its pedagogy, so he adopts it for his own LP course (p. 13); chapters 8 and 9 with 12 'alone are a good enough reason for one to buy this book' (p. 13); the final chapter is 'unique to this book', turning 'the pretty theory of the first 11 chapters magically into practical problem solving ability' (p. 14).
assumptions: Reviewer: audience and level as in problem_entry (p. 13); notes 'the often disregarded ellipsoid method' (p. 13) and the authors' 'quest for completeness of presentation' (p. 14).
proof_devices: Reviewer: the LP dual introduced through Lagrangian duality, 'highly pedagogically efficient', then the duality theorems via simplex and via convex analysis (p. 13)
Reviewer: driving artificial variables out of the basis, 'an oft ignored aspect'; worst- and average-case complexity of simplex; diameters of polyhedra (p. 13)
Reviewer: the ellipsoid method for exponentially many constraints with an efficient separation oracle 'well emphasized' (p. 13)
Reviewer: the Gomory convergence proof omitted, 'apparently owing to space limitations' (p. 14)
Reviewer: vital but easily derived results posed as exercises, e.g. Caratheodory's and Clark's theorems (p. 14)
experiments: n/a; the reviewer lists ch. 12's modeling languages, software libraries, preprocessing, choice of algorithms, effective heuristics and 'other practical tidbits' (p. 14).
positioning: No other textbook named; recommended to 'all teachers, researchers and practitioners of mathematical programming' (p. 14). Route to 05-peer-critique: its section 6 (Domains where no critique was found) no longer applies to the LO textbook. The publisher quotes three praising sentences and none of the criticisms (B002 p. 1).
writing: Reviewer on the book's writing: geometric and intuitive explanations 'widely successful' (Quote 1), e.g. a ch. 4 device picturing dual feasible bases in the primal space; insights 'seasoned math programmers grasp over the course of their research careers'; at times the phraseology 'takes the tone of a research paper' and the material 'feels dense'; style 'pleasant and to-the-point', chapter organization 'nearly ideal' (p. 14).
limits_future: Reviewer's criticisms: (1) upper-bounded simplex 'the only missing aspect' (p. 13); (2) network simplex for the uncapacitated case first, he would treat the capacitated case first (p. 13); (3) ch. 7 covers too many topics (Quote 2, p. 13); (4) ch. 6 'rather brisk but is sufficient' (p. 13); (5) ch. 11: Gomory proof omitted, branch-and-bound, branch-and-cut and knapsack DP 'briefly presented', a complexity-classes section 'out of the blue' (p. 14); (6) dense in places (p. 14). Comparisons (card's): ch. 7 is the longest chapter, 94 pp. (B004), designed as a menu by the authors (B001 p. 1); the 'out of the blue' section is 11.8 (B004 p. 5), absent from the web contents (B002 p. 2); omissions 1 and 5 fit the preface's 'comprehensive, but economical' stance [inferred]. No reply by the authors known.

method_links.note: [observed] A peer finds the stated philosophy (B001 p. 1) carried out: geometric and intuitive explanations widely successful (Quote 1); reviewer's voice, not the authors' claim.

Develop the general (capacitated) case first, then specialize (the reviewer's advice, p. 13).

quotes.text: Throughout the book, the authors make serious efforts to give geometric and intuitive explanations of various algebraic concepts, and they are widely successful in this effort.
In trying to cover too many topics in one chapter, I feel that the authors have somewhat compromised the clarity of exposition in this chapter.
